title: Explorer resolves every prevout/spender by reading and Borsh-decoding a whole block, with a per-output (not per-request) budget
why_it_is_wrong:
`find_transaction` (lookup.rs:152-176) answers "give me one transaction" by calling `chain.block(&location.block_hash)` — `Store::get_block` opens a fresh redb read transaction and Borsh-decodes the ENTIRE block (up to `max_block_size` = 1 000 000 B) to pull out one tx. Three unauthenticated explorer routes call it in a loop with no per-request work budget:

* `explorer.rs:227-231` (`GET /api/tx/{txid}`): for EVERY output not in the UTXO set it calls `find_spender`, which walks up to `SPEND_SCAN_LIMIT = 500` address-history rows and calls `find_transaction` on each. The 500 cap is per output, so the request cost is `outputs x 500` full-block decodes.
* `explorer.rs:142-150` (`GET /api/block/{id}`): `tx_fee` -> `resolve_prevouts` -> one `find_transaction` per input of every tx in the block. A historical block's inputs are all spent, so every one falls through to a full-block decode.
* `address.rs:159-183` (`GET /api/address/{a}`): one `find_transaction` per history row, up to `ADDRESS_SCAN_LIMIT = 250 000` rows, plus `resolve_prevouts` per row.

The explorer listener (`server.rs:spawn_explorer_server`) has no connection cap, no concurrency limit and no rate limit — only `POST /api/faucet` is limited. Each request runs on `context::blocking` -> `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, sharing the default 512-thread blocking pool with `Relay::accept_block` and `SyncManager`, so saturating it also stops consensus work.
concrete_failure: With `--index` (the documented deployment: RUNNING.md line 37, devnet/lib.sh:140) and mainnet params, one `GET /api/tx/<txid>` for a confirmed transaction with 100 already-spent outputs performs 100 x 500 = 50 000 `find_transaction` calls; each opens a redb read txn and Borsh-decodes a whole 1 MB block => ~50 GB of decode work and ~50 000 read transactions for a single HTTP GET, holding one blocking thread for minutes. `GET /api/block/<h>` on a full 1 MB block (~5 000 inputs) costs ~5 000 full-block decodes. ~500 concurrent such GETs from one client pin all 512 blocking threads, so `validate_gossip -> blocking(relay.accept_block)` (node/src/node/tasks.rs:246) queues behind them and the node stops validating and forwarding blocks.
suggested_fix: Give `find_transaction` a way to fetch a single transaction without materialising the block (store a byte offset/length in `TxLocation`, or add a `Store::get_tx_at(block, index)` that decodes lazily), and add a per-request work budget shared across all outputs/rows rather than a per-output `SPEND_SCAN_LIMIT`. Independently, put a `tower::limit::ConcurrencyLimitLayer` / connection cap on the explorer router, and run explorer work on a bounded semaphore so it cannot exhaust the blocking pool that block validation uses.

title: A reorg onto a branch whose bodies have not arrived marks the whole honest branch permanently Invalid
why_it_is_wrong: `execute_reorg` treats *every* failure of `connect_tip_block` as a consensus verdict about the candidate branch and calls `mark_branch_invalid(store, &plan.connect, hash)`, which writes `BlockStatus::Invalid` into the `headers` table for the failing block and every block after it in `plan.connect`. But `plan_reorg` walks headers only (`crates/chain/src/reorg.rs:96-140`) and never checks `BlockStatus::has_data()`, while `connect_tip_block` starts with `store.get_block(hash)?.ok_or(ChainError::MissingBlockBody(*hash))` (reorg.rs:153). "I have not downloaded this body yet" is therefore recorded as "this block is invalid forever". Nothing in the codebase ever calls `BlockStatus::has_data()` — it is dead code — so there is no guard anywhere on the path. `Invalid` is defined as permanent and inherited (`crates/storage/src/tables.rs:125-127`), and both `ChainManager::accept_locked` (manager.rs:404) and `accept_header` (manager.rs:214-221) refuse anything touching it with `ChainError::KnownInvalid`.
concrete_failure: Headers-first sync stores up to 2000 headers per round before any body is fetched (`crates/node/src/sync.rs:212-258`). Node tip = 500; headers accepted to 2000; bodies downloaded to 500. A miner gossips block 2001. `validate_gossip` -> `relay.accept_block` -> `accept_locked`: the parent header (2000) is known, so it is not an orphan; total work is greater, so `is_better` is true; `prev_hash != incumbent.hash`, so `reorganise(500, 2001)` runs. `plan_reorg` yields disconnect = [], connect = [501..2001]. `connect_tip_block(501)` returns `MissingBlockBody`, `roll_back` is a no-op, and `mark_branch_invalid` writes `Invalid` onto headers 501 through 2001 — the entire honest chain. From then on: when the sync path finally serves block 501's body, `accept_locked` returns `KnownInvalid` -> `block_verdict` = `GossipVerdict::Reject` (`crates/node/src/relay.rs:178`) -> `connect_blocks_from` calls `self.misbehaved(peer, ...)` and bans the honest peer; and every new header on that chain fails `accept_header` with `KnownInvalid`, which `header_failure_is_bannable` (`crates/node/src/sync/types.rs:100`) also treats as bannable. The node bans every peer serving the majority chain and can never leave height 500 without a full reindex. Minimal repro without sync: tip at height N with headers for N+1 and N+2; deliver only N+2's body; N+1 and N+2 are marked Invalid, and N+1's body is rejected when it arrives.
suggested_fix: Split the failure classes. Before executing, verify every hash in `plan.connect` has `status.has_data()` and abort the reorg with a distinct, non-recording error (e.g. `ChainError::MissingBlockBody`) if not — that is what `has_data()` exists for. In `execute_reorg`, only call `mark_branch_invalid` when the error is `ChainError::Validation(_)` or `ChainError::Consensus(_)`; storage and missing-data errors must leave the branch's status untouched.

title: Change is paid to an address no caller ever queries: every send silently strands the change
why_it_is_wrong: `plan_transaction` (wallet.rs:393) sends change to `current_change_address()`, which derives `m/44'/7767'/0'/1/next_change_index` — the *next unissued* change index. But `change_addresses()` (wallet.rs:289) enumerates `0..next_change_index`, i.e. only *already issued* ones. Nothing in the production tree ever calls `new_change_address()` (grep: only `crates/wallet/tests/wallet_api.rs` does), so `next_change_index` is永 0, `current_change_address()` is always change/0, and `change_addresses()` is always empty. Both callers that build a UTXO query list do it as `addresses() + change_addresses()`: `crates/cli/src/commands/wallet.rs:359-360` (`sync_from_node`) and `crates/rpc/src/faucet.rs:332-333` (`WalletFaucetSource::scripts`). So the one script the wallet actually pays change to is the one script it never asks the node about. `Wallet::sync` would accept the coin (the script index covers change/0 within the gap limit) — it is simply never handed it. As a second consequence, since the index never advances, every transaction the wallet ever builds pays change to the same address, linking the wallet's whole history.
concrete_failure:
1. `chain-cli wallet new` → receive/0 = A. `next_receive_index=1`, `next_change_index=0`.
2. Mine one 50 FRM coinbase to A; wait out maturity. `chain-cli wallet balance` → 50 FRM.
3. `chain-cli wallet send --to <bob> --amount 1.0` → tx spends A's coin, out[0]=1 FRM to bob, out[1]=~48.99 FRM to change/0.
4. The block confirms.
5. `chain-cli wallet balance` → `sync_from_node` queries only [A] (change list is empty); `listunspent A` returns nothing because A's coin is spent. Prints **0.00000000 FRM**.
6. `chain-cli wallet send ...` → `spendable_coins` is empty → `InsufficientFunds`. The 48.99 FRM is unspendable through the CLI forever; recovery requires `dump-seed` into another implementation.
Same shape in `WalletFaucetSource`: after its first payment, `scripts()` no longer covers where the change went, `utxos_for_scripts` returns empty, and every later request answers `FaucetDrained` permanently.
suggested_fix: Make the change address the wallet reports and the change address it pays to the same thing. Either have `send`/`plan_transaction` issue and persist a fresh change index (rotating per transaction, which also fixes the reuse), or at minimum include `current_change_address()` in `change_addresses()` / in both callers' query lists. A regression test should be: fund → send → re-sync → assert the change is visible and spendable.

title: genesis_commitment omits bft_activation_height and bft_validators, so a mis-set fork schedule produces an identical genesis hash and a silent permanent split
why_it_is_wrong: genesis_commitment() is the mechanism that makes "a difference anywhere in the consensus parameters is a different genesis block and an immediate, loud disagreement" (its own doc comment). It hashes chain_id, spacing, halflife, pow_limit, subsidy, halving_interval, coinbase_maturity, max_block_size, median_time_span, genesis timestamp/bits/nonce — and stops there. It does NOT cover params.bft_activation_height or params.bft_validators, which are the two most consensus-critical values in the whole set: they decide which ConsensusEngine validates every block at and above the fork height (EngineRouter::engine_for_height / ChainParams::engine_at), and validators.rs itself says "the order of ChainParams::bft_validators is consensus-critical: reordering the list is a hard fork". Both are loaded per-node from a --consensus-config TOML (crates/node/src/config/resolve.rs:547 apply_consensus_file), so they are exactly the kind of value that can differ between two nodes that believe they are on the same network. There is also no genesis-hash exchange in the p2p handshake, so nothing else catches it either. This is the same defect shape as the old height-1 ASERT anchor: a consensus rule parameterised by something that is not pinned identically on every node, with no detection until the chain has already forked.
concrete_failure: Operator rolls out BFT to a 4-node mainnet. Nodes A and B get consensus.toml with `bft_activation_height = 500000` and the validator list; node C's rollout is missed (or its file has the validators in a different order). All three compute the identical genesis hash from ChainParams::mainnet(), so init_genesis succeeds everywhere, `getblockchaininfo` shows the same genesis, and they sync normally to height 499 999. At height 500 000 A and B produce/require a block with BlockSeal::ENGINE_BFT and a 2f+1 certificate; C's engine_for_height(500000) returns PowEngine, whose validate_seal rejects it with ConsensusError::WrongEngine { expected: 0, actual: 1 }, and ChainManager::accept_locked records the block Invalid, so C can never accept that branch even after the config is fixed. Conversely C's PoW block at 500 000 is rejected by A and B. Two honest, correctly-running nodes fork permanently, with no startup error and nothing in the genesis check to warn anyone. (Validator-order mismatch is worse still: genesis matches, activation matches, and the split only appears when a commit signed by validator index i is verified against a different key.)
suggested_fix: Fold the fork schedule into the commitment: append `bft_activation_height` (e.g. u64::MAX for None, so today's None-valued networks keep their published hashes only if that encoding is chosen deliberately) and each ValidatorId's 32 bytes in index order, then republish the genesis hashes in RUNNING.md. If changing the mainnet genesis hash is unacceptable, add a second, separately-checked `consensus_schedule_commitment` that peers exchange in the p2p handshake and refuse to peer on mismatch — the point is that the value must be checked network-wide before the fork height, not discovered at it.

title: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY enforces no relative timelock — nothing compares the input's sequence against the spent coin's age
why_it_is_wrong: check_sequence() validates the script operand only against ctx.tx.inputs[input_index].sequence — a field the *spender* writes freely. That is correct BIP-112 script-half behaviour, but BIP-112 is only a timelock because BIP-68 separately requires the chain to check that `sequence` is actually satisfied by the age of the coin being spent (coin.height vs block height, or coin's MTP vs block MTP). That second half does not exist anywhere in Ferrum: `grep -rn 'SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME|sequence_lock|relative_lock' crates/ --include=*.rs` outside crates/script returns nothing but a comment in crates/wallet/src/build.rs:49. crates/chain/src/apply.rs validates coinbase maturity (line 110), absolute finality via is_final (line 156) and scripts (line 171), and never looks at TxIn::sequence except inside is_final's all-final shortcut (crates/chain/src/validate.rs:237). crates/mempool/src/pool/accept.rs is the same. Coin carries `height`, so the data is there and simply unused. SPEC §4.4 documents only the script-side rule, so the omission is not flagged as deliberate in DECISIONS.md either.
concrete_failure: Create a UTXO whose script_pubkey is `<0x0a> OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY OP_DROP <32B pk> OP_CHECKSIG` (a 10-block relative lock) at height H. In block H+1, spend it with an input whose `sequence = 10` and a valid signature. check_sequence reads operand 10, sees 10 < 2^31 so no disable-flag error, `10 & SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_TYPE_FLAG == 10 & TYPE_FLAG` so no type mismatch, and `10 & 0xffff <= 10 & 0xffff` so no UnsatisfiedSequence — the opcode passes. is_final is unaffected (lock_time can be 0). apply_block accepts the block. The coin was one block old, not ten: the relative timelock never happened. Every CSV-based construction — the refund leg of a channel, a vault delay, `<n> OP_CSV OP_DROP` in a redeem script — is spendable immediately by whoever can sign.
suggested_fix: Add a BIP-68 sequence-lock check to the contextual transaction rules in crates/chain/src/apply.rs (and mirror it in mempool accept): for each input whose `sequence & SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_DISABLE_FLAG == 0`, compute the coin's minimum spend height (coin.height + (sequence & MASK) + 1) or minimum spend time (MTP of coin.height's block + ((sequence & MASK) << 9) + 1) depending on SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_TYPE_FLAG, and reject the transaction unless ctx.height / ctx.median_time_past_s satisfies it. Add the rule to SPEC §4.4 so a second implementer cannot repeat the omission, and add a chain-level test that spends a `<n> OP_CSV` output one block early and expects rejection.

title: select_for_block is O(chain-depth x pool size) storage lookups with the mempool mutex held; no ancestor/descendant limit exists
why_it_is_wrong:
`select_for_block` runs repeated passes over the candidate list and includes a transaction only when its parent is already in the overlay; anything whose parent is still `waiting` is deferred to the next pass (select.rs:112-146). Candidates arrive in descending fee-rate order (`pool.rs:222-236`, `by_fee.iter().rev()`). For a chain where each child pays a higher rate than its parent, the descending order is exactly reverse-dependency order, so every pass includes exactly ONE transaction and defers the rest: N passes over ~N candidates. Each deferred check costs an `OverlayView::get_coin` miss that falls through to `Store::get_coin`, i.e. a fresh redb read transaction (storage/src/view.rs:180-186, store/reads.rs:80).

Ferrum has no ancestor/descendant count limit anywhere in `crates/mempool` (Bitcoin Core's 25-ancestor rule has no counterpart here), so chain depth is bounded only by `max_bytes` = 8 MiB. Worse, `Mempool::select_for_block` takes `self.inner.lock()` at pool.rs:228 and holds it for the whole selection.
concrete_failure: Broadcast a chain of 30 000 chained 200-byte transactions t0 -> t1 -> ... -> t29999 with strictly ascending fee rate (child pays 1 grain/kB more than its parent). That is ~6 MB (under the 8 MiB `max_bytes`) and ~6 000 000 grains ≈ 0.06 FRM in total fees. The fee index orders them t29999 first, so pass k defers 30000-k candidates and includes only t(k-1): ~4.5x10^8 `Store::get_coin` redb read transactions per `select_for_block` call. The miner calls it at the start of every round (`node/src/miner.rs:build_template`), and it holds the mempool `Mutex` throughout — so `Relay::accept_transaction` (mempool.accept) and, critically, `Relay::on_accepted -> mempool.remove_confirmed` both block, which stalls block acceptance for the duration. Existing tests only cover a three-deep chain (`select_tests.rs:65`).
suggested_fix: Cap ancestor/descendant chain length and total ancestor size at admission (e.g. 25 / 101 kvB as policy), and/or make selection topological in one pass: build the parent->child map from `Inner::spent` once and process a candidate only after its in-pool parents, instead of re-scanning the whole pending list each pass. Also drop the mempool lock before the storage-heavy part by snapshotting the candidate entries.

title: Mempool orphans can never expire: promote_orphans re-inserts each failed orphan with the current tip height
why_it_is_wrong:
`OrphanPool::expire` (orphan.rs:220-228) drops entries where `tip_height - e.added_height >= expiry_blocks`. `Mempool::promote_orphans` (pool.rs:286-311) — called from `Relay::after_tip_move` (node/src/relay.rs:529) on every accepted block — `take`s every orphan out of the pool and re-runs `insert_one`; an orphan whose parents are still missing is re-orphaned at accept.rs:109 with `added_height = tip_height`, i.e. the CURRENT height. So after each block every surviving orphan's age resets to 0 and `expire` can never fire. `OrphanPool::insert`'s own doc claims "a peer cannot renew an orphan indefinitely by resending it" — the node renews them itself.

Compounding this, orphan admission is free: `insert_one` resolves inputs (step 7) *before* the fee floor (step 9) and script verification (step 10), so an orphan needs no valid signature, no fee and no real UTXO — only `check_transaction_sanity` and `check_standard` (size <= 100 000 B, push-only script_sig, standard outputs), all of which an empty `script_sig` satisfies.
concrete_failure: Gossip 200 transactions (the `DEFAULT_MAX_ORPHANS` ceiling), each 100 000 B with ~2 270 minimal inputs (44 B each: 32-byte random txid, vout, empty push-only script_sig, sequence) naming txids that will never exist, plus one standard output. All 200 are admitted to the orphan pool for free. From then on, every block connect runs `promote_orphans`, which re-resolves 200 x 2 270 ≈ 454 000 inputs — each a `Store::get_coin` redb read transaction — under the mempool `Mutex`, on the block-acceptance path, and re-stamps `added_height` to the new tip so `expire` never collects them. The pool stays permanently full, so every legitimate orphan is evicted, and the ~1-3 s per block of locked-mempool work repeats forever from a single 20 MB upload.
suggested_fix: Preserve the original `added_height` (and `seq`) when re-orphaning inside `promote_orphans` — pass the entry's own `added_height` through, or restore it after `insert_one` returns `Orphaned`. Additionally bound the orphan pool by bytes as well as count, and cap the number of missing parents an orphan may name so the re-resolution cost per block is bounded.

title: The p2p event loop awaits the serve semaphore inline, so a peer streaming GetBlocks stops the node draining gossip
why_it_is_wrong: `run_p2p` (tasks.rs:170-181) processes events strictly serially: `handle_event(&ctx, &serves, event).await`. For `P2pEvent::InboundRequest`, `handle_event` does `Arc::clone(serves).acquire_owned().await` (line 215) *before* spawning the serve task. When all `MAX_CONCURRENT_SERVES = 8` permits are held, the event loop itself parks on that await and stops calling `events.recv()` — so nothing else in the channel is drained either. This directly contradicts the module's stated design (tasks.rs:23-26: "a peer doing initial sync must not stall block relay for everyone else"). There is no per-peer cap on `pending_inbound` in the p2p worker (only the global `MAX_PENDING_INBOUND_REQUESTS = 128`), and one connection may open `MAX_CONCURRENT_SYNC_STREAMS = 16` sync streams.
concrete_failure: A single peer keeps a continuous stream of `GetBlocks` requests for 64 known block hashes outstanding. Each serve reads 64 blocks from redb (see the separate `bodies` finding) and takes on the order of hundreds of milliseconds. With 128 requests parked, gossip events sit behind them in the same FIFO and are delayed by ~16 serve-times; because the loop is parked on `acquire_owned` it is not draining at all, so the 1024-slot event channel fills and `Worker::emit_or_return` (p2p/src/service/worker.rs:243-256) starts shedding `P2pEvent::Gossip`. A shed gossip message is never validated, so `report_validation` is never called — and gossipsub is in explicit-validation mode (`config.rs: .validate_messages()`), so the block is neither accepted locally nor forwarded. One peer turns the node into a black hole for block propagation at zero cost.
suggested_fix: Do not await the permit in the event loop. Either `serves.try_acquire_owned()` and drop the responder (libp2p reports a response omission, which the peer retries) when the pool is busy, or move `InboundRequest` events onto their own bounded queue drained by a separate task so gossip and sync-serving cannot head-of-line-block each other.

title: `pol_round` is outside the signed proposal digest, and the first proposal per round is cached forever — any relay can halt the chain permanently
why_it_is_wrong: `Proposal::sign` (vote.rs:186-204) signs only `proposal_digest(VoteMsg{chain_id, height, round, block_hash})`; `pol_round` is deliberately excluded and `Proposal::verify` (vote.rs:212-214) therefore accepts any `pol_round` value on an otherwise-genuine, correctly-signed proposal. The doc comment justifies this with "a proposer that lies about `pol_round` achieves nothing", but that only reasons about the *proposer* over-claiming a polka. It does not cover a third party *downgrading* or *poisoning* the field, and the receive path makes that fatal: `on_proposal` (machine.rs:237-251) inserts the first proposal seen for a round and then permanently discards every later one — a later copy with the same `block_hash` is not even flagged as equivocation, it is silently counted as `ignored`. So the mutated copy that arrives first is the copy every rule is evaluated against for the rest of that round. `try_prevote_on_proposal` then takes `pol_round` at face value as a control input: `Some(vr)` with `vr >= round` returns `false` (machine.rs:450-453), meaning the node never prevotes in that round at all and just waits out the propose timeout; `None` forces the rule-2 branch (machine.rs:440-446), which makes every locked validator prevote nil for a block it would otherwise have unlocked onto.
concrete_failure: n=4, height 1, round 0. Proposer v1 broadcasts `Proposal{height:1, round:0, block_hash:B, pol_round:None, proposer:1, sig}`. An attacker with no validator key at all copies that message, sets `pol_round: Some(0)`, and gets it to v0, v2, v3 first (the signature still verifies — `proposal_digest` never covered the field). Each honest node caches the poisoned copy in `proposals[0]`; the genuine copy arriving later hits the `Entry::Occupied` arm, matches on `block_hash`, and is dropped. `try_prevote_on_proposal` hits `vr = 0 >= round = 0` and returns false on this and every subsequent event, so nobody ever prevotes B. The propose timer expires, all four prevote nil, nil-polka precommits nil, the precommit timer expires, round 1 starts — and the attacker repeats. No block is ever produced at any height, by an adversary holding zero keys. The same primitive also works as a downgrade after a lock: strip `pol_round: Some(6)` to `None` on a round-7 re-proposal of B and every validator locked on A takes the rule-2 branch, prevotes nil, and the polka for B can never be acted on.
suggested_fix: Put `pol_round` inside the signed preimage (a second, distinct tagged digest for proposals keeps `VoteMsg` frozen at 48 bytes: sign `tagged_hash(TAG_BFT_PROPOSAL, borsh(VoteMsg) || borsh(Option<u32>))`). Until then, at minimum: (a) key the `proposals` cache on `(round, block_hash, pol_round)` or replace a cached entry when a same-`block_hash` proposal arrives with a *usable* `pol_round` that the cached one lacked, so a poisoned copy cannot win by arriving first; and (b) treat `vr >= round` as "this round has no usable proposal" and prevote nil immediately rather than silently returning false and burning the full propose timeout.

title: Votes are buffered for unbounded rounds and every event rescans all of them — one Byzantine validator wedges every node with quadratic CPU and unbounded memory
why_it_is_wrong: `on_vote` (machine.rs:255-282) validates only `started`, `chain_id`, `height` and the signature. `signed.vote.round` is completely unconstrained: any `u32` is accepted and `VoteTally::add` (state.rs:281-290) creates a fresh `RoundVotes` bucket for it via `entry(round).or_default()`. Nothing prunes rounds within a height — `VoteTally::clear` runs only on `reset_to_height`. Every accepted vote then calls `advance` (machine.rs:280), which runs up to `MAX_ADVANCE_PASSES = 16` passes of `advance_once`, and each pass does two full scans of the whole round space: `decided()` (state.rs:323-327) iterates every precommit round and calls `quorum_block` on each, and `skip_round()` (state.rs:346-360) *allocates a fresh `BTreeSet<u32>` containing every prevote and precommit round above the current one* on every single call. So the per-event cost is O(R) where R is the number of distinct rounds an attacker has seeded, and seeding R votes costs O(R²). This is squarely inside the stated threat model: n=4 tolerates f=1 Byzantine validator, and the design promise is that the chain *halts gracefully*, not that honest nodes are driven into CPU/memory exhaustion.
concrete_failure: n=4 (f=1, quorum=3). Validator 3 is Byzantine. At the current height h it signs and sends 100,000 precommits for NIL_BLOCK, one at each of rounds 1..100,000 (all trivially valid: correct chain_id, correct height, correct BIP-340 signature over `precommit_digest`, its own index). Each one passes `on_vote`, lands in a new `RoundVotes` bucket, returns `VoteOutcome::Accepted`, and triggers `advance`. Nil votes never satisfy `quorum_block` (which filters `!block.is_zero()`) and a single voter never reaches the f+1=2 `skip_round` threshold, so every pass runs to completion: by vote k the machine allocates and walks a ~k-element BTreeSet up to 16 times, plus a k-round `decided()` scan. Cumulative work is ~16·Σk ≈ 8×10^10 BTreeSet operations for ~11 MB of attacker traffic, and the machine holds 100,000 live `RoundVotes` allocations. Every honest validator *and* every non-voting full node running the same machine stops making progress — not a quorum halt, a resource kill, and the votes are indistinguishable from legitimate ones so there is nothing to ban on.
suggested_fix: Reject in `on_vote` (and `on_proposal`) any message whose round is outside a bounded window around `state.round` — e.g. `round <= state.round.saturating_add(LOOKAHEAD)` with a small LOOKAHEAD, which is all rule 12 needs since `skip_round` only ever advances to the *lowest* qualifying round. Additionally, drop round buckets strictly below `state.round` once the round advances (nothing reads them except `polka(vr, ..)` for `vr < round`, which needs only the retained `valid_round`/lock window), and make `skip_round` scan with `range((Excluded(current), Unbounded))` instead of building a full BTreeSet.

title: A 6-validator set is accepted with only a log warning, and its two disjoint quorums let one Byzantine proposer commit two different blocks at one height
why_it_is_wrong: `quorum()` returns `2f+1` with `f = (n-1)/3`, which for n=6 gives f=1, quorum=3 — and 2·3 = 6 is *not* > 6, so two disjoint quorums exist. `has_quorum_intersection()` (validators.rs:123-125) computes exactly this, and `quorum_intersection_holds_for_every_set_size_except_six` in tests/commit.rs:136 asserts n=6 is the single degenerate size. But nothing refuses it: `ValidatorSet::new` has no such check, and `BftEngine::new` (engine.rs:58-64) only emits `tracing::warn!` and proceeds. `EngineRouter::new`'s own doc claims it errors "when the configured set cannot form a quorum", which is not what the code does. Quorum intersection is the *entire* basis for the promises in SPEC 9.2 and RUNNING.md ("this chain may halt for up to 24 hours; it will never fork") and for `EngineRouter::check_reorg`'s justification ("by quorum intersection no conflicting block at that height can ever gather 2f+1 of its own"). A configuration that provably breaks that with only f=1 Byzantine validator should be a boot failure, not a log line an operator scrolls past.
concrete_failure: `bft_validators` has 6 keys; f=1, quorum=3. At height h round 0 the proposer is validator 5 = (h+0) mod 6, and validator 5 is the single Byzantine node (within tolerance). It signs two round-0 proposals and gossips Proposal(A) to {0,1,2} and Proposal(B) to {3,4}. Honest 0,1,2 prevote A (3 votes = quorum), so `try_lock_on_polka` locks them on A and each precommits A. Honest 3,4 prevote B and Byzantine 5 also prevotes B (3 votes = quorum), so 3,4 lock on B and precommit B, and 5 precommits B. Precommits for A at round 0 = {0,1,2} = 3 = quorum → `decided()` fires and 0,1,2 emit `Decide(A)`. Precommits for B at round 0 = {3,4,5} = 3 = quorum → 3,4 emit `Decide(B)`. Two different blocks are decided at height h, and both certificates pass `verify_commit` and therefore `validate_seal` — a hard chain fork produced by exactly one faulty validator, on a set size the constructor accepts.
suggested_fix: Make `ValidatorSet::new` (or at least `BftEngine::new`) return an error — a new `ConsensusError` variant, e.g. `NoQuorumIntersection { validators, quorum }` — when `!has_quorum_intersection()`, so a 6-validator set is a startup failure. Keep the `2f+1` formula exactly as the contract specifies; only the accepted set sizes change, and 4/5/7/8/… are all still admissible.

title: BlockStatus::HaveData is committed in its own transaction before the body it claims exists
why_it_is_wrong:
`accept_locked` writes the index entry with `status: BlockStatus::HaveData` in one redb write transaction and the body in a second, separate one:
```rust
self.store.store_header(&entry)?;        // txn 1: status = HaveData, committed+fsynced
self.store.store_block_body(&hash, &block)?;  // txn 2
```
This is exactly the "pointer written before the data it names" ordering that `Store::connect_block` was carefully built to avoid (see the module doc in `crates/storage/src/store.rs:1-19`), applied to a different pointer. redb's default durability is `Immediate`, so txn 1 is on disk before txn 2 even starts. Worse, the resulting state is self-concealing: `accept_locked`'s duplicate short-circuit (manager.rs:405) returns `AcceptOutcome::Duplicate` for `HaveData`, and `SyncManager::accept_headers` computes `have_body` from the same status (`crates/node/src/sync.rs:305-312`) and therefore never puts the hash in `wanted`. Nothing ever re-requests or re-stores the body.
concrete_failure: Power cut (or a full disk making `store_block_body` return `StorageError::Db`) between the two commits, for a block B at height H. On restart the `headers` table says B is `HaveData`; the `blocks` table has no row for B. Sync never asks for B's body again (`have_body` is true), and any peer re-gossiping B gets `Duplicate`. If B is on the active chain's front, `connect_tip_block(B)` fails with `MissingBlockBody` forever and the node stalls at H-1; if B is on a competing branch, the first reorg through it hits `MissingBlockBody` and — via finding 1 — marks the branch Invalid. Only `chain reindex` (which cannot help, since the body is genuinely gone) or wiping the datadir recovers.
suggested_fix: Store the body first and the header second (`store_block_body` then `store_header`), so a crash leaves an orphaned body — harmless and re-writable — rather than a status that lies. Better: add a `Store` method that writes body and header in one write transaction, which is what the invariant in `store.rs` already argues for. Additionally, make the sync `have_body` probe check `store.get_block(&hash)?.is_some()` rather than trusting the status byte.

title: A transient storage error permanently marks a valid block Invalid
why_it_is_wrong: `accept_locked` maps *any* error from `connect_tip_block` to `self.mark_invalid(&hash)`, and `execute_reorg` maps any connect error to `mark_branch_invalid` (reorg.rs:235). `connect_tip_block` can fail for reasons that say nothing about the block: `store.connect_block` returns `StorageError::Db` on a redb/IO failure, `StorageError::NonContiguousConnect` and `StorageError::ParentMismatch` on a tip mismatch, and `store.get_header`/`get_block` can return `StorageError::Corrupt`. `BlockStatus::Invalid` is documented and implemented as permanent and inherited (`crates/storage/src/tables.rs:125-127`), and `relay.rs:178` maps `KnownInvalid` to `GossipVerdict::Reject`, i.e. a peer ban.
concrete_failure: The datadir fills up while the node is connecting the honest tip block B. `redb`'s commit inside `Store::connect_block` returns an IO error, `connect_tip_block` returns `ChainError::Storage(..)`, and `mark_invalid(&B)` writes `BlockStatus::Invalid` for B in its own (small, still-succeeding) transaction. The operator frees disk and restarts. The node now answers `ChainError::KnownInvalid(B)` for B and, because `accept_locked` also rejects any block whose parent is Invalid (manager.rs:417), for every descendant of B — and bans each peer that offers them. The chain is permanently stuck one block below the network, with no log line saying the verdict was caused by the disk rather than the block.
suggested_fix: Only record `BlockStatus::Invalid` for `ChainError::Validation(_)` and `ChainError::Consensus(_)` — the classes `relay::block_rejection` already calls `BlockRejection::Invalid`. For every other error, log and leave the status alone so the block is retried. `block_rejection` already draws exactly this line; reuse it at the two `mark_invalid` call sites.

title: Two `wallet send` calls in one block interval produce an identical tx; the duplicate is reported as a successful second payment
why_it_is_wrong: `Wallet::send` reserves the selected outpoints (wallet.rs:451, `coins.reserve`), and its doc claims that is "what stops a second `send` before the first confirms from selecting the same coins". In the CLI the reservation is worthless: `open_or_create` builds a fresh `Wallet` per process and the `CoinCache` dies with it. Worse, every input to the build is deterministic — `gettxout`/`listunspent` read only the confirmed UTXO set (`crates/rpc/src/adapters.rs:137` iterates `store.iter_utxos()`, no mempool), coin selection is over a `BTreeMap`, `lock_time` = tip height, `sequence` is fixed, change goes to the never-advancing change/0, and signing uses `sign_deterministic` (aux=[0;32]). So a repeat of the same command before a new block yields a **byte-identical transaction**. `insert_one` (crates/mempool/src/pool/accept.rs:72) returns `Ok(Admission::AlreadyInPool)` for a tx it already holds, `relay.accept_transaction` maps that to `error: None`, and `MempoolHandle::submit` returns `Ok(txid)`. The CLI prints the txid and exits 0.
concrete_failure:
With a funded wallet and no block mined in between:
```
$ chain-cli wallet send --to bob --amount 1.0
<txid T>            # exit 0 — bob is paid 1 FRM
$ chain-cli wallet send --to bob --amount 1.0
<txid T>            # exit 0 — bob is paid nothing more
```
A payout script doing `for i in 1 2 3; do chain-cli wallet send --to $bob --amount 1.0; done` reports three successes and transfers 1 FRM. (If the amount differs the txs differ and the second fails loudly with `MempoolError::Conflict`; it is the equal-amount case that is silent.)
suggested_fix: Persist reservations (or at least the spent outpoints of broadcast-but-unconfirmed txs) in the keystore metadata alongside the address indices, so a new process re-applies them before selection; and have `wallet send` distinguish `AlreadyInPool` from `Accepted` — `MempoolProvider::submit` should surface the admission variant so `sendrawtransaction` can tell the caller "this exact transaction was already in the pool" instead of reporting a new payment.

title: wallet.json is written with default permissions while the default passphrase is empty, so any local user can read the mnemonic
why_it_is_wrong: `Keystore::persist` writes `<datadir>/wallet.json` (and its `.tmp` sibling) with `std::fs::write`, which uses `0o666 & ~umask` — mode 0644 under the common umask 022. Every other key file in the tree is deliberately narrowed: `NodeKey::write` calls `set_owner_only` (crates/node/src/node/keys.rs:160) and `write_key_file` calls `restrict_permissions` (crates/cli/src/keyfile.rs:118). The keystore — the file that holds the *mnemonic* — is the one that gets nothing. That would be tolerable if the ciphertext were strong, but `PassphraseSource::resolve` returns the **empty string** when no flag is given (documented as deliberate for devnet automation), and `open_or_create` uses that empty passphrase to create a wallet implicitly on the first `wallet address` / `balance` / `send` / `dump-seed`. PBKDF2 with a known passphrase and a salt printed in the file is not encryption.
concrete_failure: On a shared Linux host: Alice runs `chain-cli wallet address` (no passphrase flags). A keystore appears at `~alice/.local/share/ferrum/wallet.json`, mode 0644. Bob runs `cat ~alice/.local/share/ferrum/wallet.json`, reads `kdf.salt`, `kdf.iterations`, `nonce`, `ciphertext`, runs PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512("", salt, 210000, 96) and the HMAC-SHA512-CTR keystream from the module, and recovers Alice's twelve-word mnemonic — every coin the wallet controls. No race, no privilege, no timing needed.
suggested_fix: Create the keystore (and its temp file) with `OpenOptions::new().create_new(true).mode(0o600)` on Unix before writing, mirroring what `keys.rs` and `keyfile.rs` already do — and set the permission on the temp file *before* the rename, not after. Separately, consider making `wallet new` warn loudly on stderr when it seals a keystore with the empty passphrase.

title: apply_block checks median-time-past before proof of work; SPEC, CONTRACT, PowEngine and the reference all check PoW first — the differential test cannot see it
why_it_is_wrong:
SPEC §3.2 fixes the header order as rule 8 (PoW) then rule 9 (timestamp > MTP), and calls that order normative. CONTRACT §8.1 rule 5 lists it the same way ("PoW target met; bits equals next_bits(parent); timestamp_ms > median_time_past(parent)*1000"). D:\Blockchain_Crypto\crates\consensus\src\pow.rs:174-189 follows it. D:\Blockchain_Crypto\testing\sim\src\reference.rs:213-238 follows it. Only apply.rs's private check_header inverts it: timestamp at line 242-248, then the whole PoW/target block at 250-266. So production disagrees with itself (apply_block vs PowEngine::validate_header) and with the reference executor.

The differential test is supposed to be the audit substitute for exactly this. It cannot catch it because mutate.rs is built on the stated rule "every entry breaks exactly one rule": there is a timestamp-only mutation ("the timestamp is not strictly after median time past") and a PoW-only mutation ("the header hash does not meet its target"), and no fixture anywhere pairs them. the_two_executors_agree_on_the_order_rules_are_checked_in covers five other pairs and not this one.

Same function, same blind spot: production checks version < MIN_BLOCK_VERSION at apply.rs:217 *before* the genesis exemption at 221, while reference.rs:189-197 returns Ok for genesis before ever looking at version. A genesis block with version 0 is BadVersion to production and valid to the reference. The differential test feeds genesis through agree() but only ever the real genesis, whose version is 1.
concrete_failure: In testing/sim, at any height >= 1: `let mut b = chain.build_block(&BlockPlan { timestamp_ms: Some(ctx.median_time_past_ms()), grind: false, ..Default::default() })?; grind_until_invalid(&mut b.header)?;` (both knobs already exist — plan.rs `timestamp_ms`/`grind`, mutate.rs `grind_until_invalid`). Then `apply_block` returns `Err(Header(TimestampTooOld{..}))` while `apply_block_reference` returns `Err(Header(InsufficientWork{..}))`, and `PowEngine::validate_header` on the same header returns `InsufficientWork`. Feeding that block to `agree()` in testing/sim/tests/differential.rs panics with "the two executors reject for different reasons". CI is green today only because no fixture constructs it.
suggested_fix: Move the target/pow_limit/hash_meets_target block in crates/chain/src/apply.rs::check_header above the median-time-past comparison, so it matches PowEngine::validate_header, SPEC §3.2 and the reference; move the version check below the genesis early-return. Then add a mutation family to invalid_variants (or a case to the ordering test) that breaks two header rules at once — bad timestamp + bad PoW, bad timestamp + bits above pow_limit — so the ordering is pinned rather than assumed.

title: check_transaction_sanity checks NullInput before the duplicate-input and script-size rules; SPEC §4.1 and the reference check it last
why_it_is_wrong:
SPEC §4.1 lists the bullets in this order: inputs/outputs non-empty; output values valid; output sum valid; **no duplicate OutPoint among inputs**; **script sizes**; then coinbase shape / non-coinbase null-input. testing/sim/src/reference.rs:130-168 implements exactly that: a duplicate loop over all inputs (line 132), then a script_sig size loop (138), then a script_pubkey size loop (146), then the null-input loop last (166).

Production fuses all three into one per-input loop and puts the null check first (validate.rs:120-126): NullInput, then DuplicateInput, then check_script_size, per input index. For any transaction that breaks the null rule together with either of the other two, the two implementations name different rules. SPEC §3.4 says the variant is the contract ("Tests assert the exact variant... A test that only asserts 'rejected' passes when the block is rejected for the wrong reason"), so this is observable behaviour, not formatting.

The catalogue's only null-input fixture (mutate.rs "a non-coinbase transaction names the null outpoint") uses inputs [(ZERO,6), NULL] — distinct outpoints, both script_sigs empty — which is precisely the shape where the two orders coincide. That is a fixture that makes the disagreement it would expose unreachable.
concrete_failure: A non-coinbase transaction with `inputs = [TxIn::coinbase(Script::EMPTY), TxIn::coinbase(Script::EMPTY)]` (two NULL outpoints, so `is_coinbase()` is false because len != 1) and one valid output, placed at index 1 of an otherwise honest block. `ferrum_chain::apply_block` returns `Err(NullInput { input_index: 0 })`; `apply_block_reference` returns `Err(DuplicateInput { out_point: OutPoint::NULL })`. `judge()`/`agree()` would report ExecutorDisagreement. Same divergence with `inputs = [NULL, X]` where X carries a 1001-byte script_sig: production says NullInput{0}, the reference says ScriptTooLarge.
suggested_fix: Split the loop in check_transaction_sanity into SPEC's order — duplicate-outpoint pass, then script_sig/script_pubkey size pass, then the null-input pass — or amend SPEC §4.1 and reference.rs together if the fused order is deliberate. Either way add a two-defect fixture ([NULL, NULL] and [NULL, oversized]) to invalid_variants so the choice is pinned by the differential.

title: build_template sizes candidate blocks with EMPTY_SEAL_SIZE = 5 even at BFT heights, so a full BFT block is over max_block_size the moment the certificate is attached
why_it_is_wrong: block_size_of() hard-codes `BLOCK_FIXED_OVERHEAD + EMPTY_SEAL_SIZE` (92 + 5) and build_template uses it as the budget against params.max_block_size (template.rs:136, 148-152). But the block that is actually sealed at a BFT height carries `BlockSeal::bft(commit.encode())`: borsh(BftCommit) is height(8) + round(4) + block_hash(32) + Vec len(4) + quorum*(u16 + 64-byte Signature) = 48 + 66*q bytes, and BlockSeal::borsh_size adds 5. For the minimum set n=4, q=3 that is 251 bytes where the template budgeted 5 — a 246-byte undercount, growing by 66 bytes per extra validator. Block::serialized_size() (types/block.rs:302) counts seal.borsh_size(), and SPEC §3.1 rule 1 / check_block_sanity (validate.rs:177) enforce it. The miner is engine-agnostic — miner.rs:174 picks the engine for the height and calls engine.seal(template) — so nothing between the budget and the seal re-checks the size. The `debug_assert_eq!` at template.rs:190 does not catch it because it deliberately constructs the comparison block with `BlockSeal::POW`.
concrete_failure: BFT is active, n = 4 (quorum 3), max_block_size = 1_000_000, mempool is full. build_template packs transactions until block_size_of(txs) == 1_000_000 and returns the template. BftEngine::seal attaches a 3-signature certificate, so the resulting Block::serialized_size() is 1_000_246. The proposer hands it to Relay::accept_block -> ChainManager::accept_block -> check_block_sanity, which returns ValidationError::BlockTooLarge { size: 1000246, max: 1000000 }. Every other validator rejects it identically, no block is committed at that height, and because the mempool contents are unchanged the next round rebuilds the same over-large template — the chain halts at that height until the mempool drains below the limit. (With n = 7 the overshoot is 378+5 bytes and the failure is the same.)
suggested_fix: Make the seal budget engine-dependent: pass the active engine's worst-case seal size into build_template (PoW = 5; BFT = 5 + 48 + 66 * validator_count, not just the quorum, since verify_commit accepts up to n signatures) and subtract it from max_block_size before selecting transactions. Also change the debug_assert to build the comparison Block with the seal the active engine will actually produce, so the accounting mismatch fails a test instead of a block.

title: SPEC §3.1 rule 1 measures the BFT seal, which the block hash does not commit to and which verify_commit lets vary between quorum and n signatures
why_it_is_wrong: Block::serialized_size() includes self.seal.borsh_size(), and check_block_sanity (validate.rs:177) rejects the block when that exceeds max_block_size. DECISIONS D2 states explicitly that the seal is outside the header so that "the block hash is identical no matter which 2f+1 subset of signatures a given node happened to collect" — i.e. the seal is by design a non-committed, malleable field. BftEngine::verify_commit (bft/engine.rs:252) only requires `commit.signatures.len() >= quorum` with strictly ascending indices; it happily accepts any count up to n. So one block hash has up to (n - quorum) legal seal sizes, each 66 bytes apart, and whether it passes rule 1 depends on which one a node happened to receive. That makes a consensus rule a function of a value the block does not commit to — the same class of defect as a fork-dependent difficulty anchor, just via the wire form instead of the chain.
concrete_failure: n = 7, quorum = 5, max_block_size = 1_000_000. A proposer commits a block whose txs plus a 5-signature seal total 999_950 bytes; node A receives that copy and accepts it (rule 1 passes at 999_950). A relaying peer — precommit votes are gossiped, so anyone can collect them — re-encodes the same block with all 7 valid signatures (seal grows by 2*66 = 132 bytes) and gossips it; because the gossipsub message id is a content hash the modified copy propagates as a distinct message. Node B receives only that copy: serialized_size() = 1_000_082, check_block_sanity returns BlockTooLarge, accept_locked propagates the error before the block is ever stored, and B stays on the parent while A has advanced. Two honest nodes disagree about the validity of one block hash, and the attacker needed no validator key.
suggested_fix: Take the seal out of rule 1: measure `HEADER_SIZE + 4 + sum(tx.borsh_size())` against max_block_size and bound the seal separately with its own engine-specific cap (e.g. reject a BFT seal longer than 5 + 48 + 66*n). Alternatively canonicalise the certificate before storing/relaying — truncate to exactly the lowest `quorum` indices — so one block hash has exactly one seal encoding.

title: The sighash mid-state digests are recomputed on every signature check, so script validation is quadratic in transaction size — the opposite of what the module documents
why_it_is_wrong: check_signature() calls signature_hash(...) directly, which calls sighash_preimage(), which recomputes hash_prevouts(tx) (crates/script/src/sighash.rs:189), hash_sequences(tx) (:193) and hash_outputs(tx, ..) (:195) from scratch every single time. There is no cache: Machine holds only { ctx, stack, altstack, ops, sig_checks, max_stack } (crates/script/src/interpreter.rs:111-118) and ExecCtx carries no precomputed digests (:51-67). hash_prevouts hashes 36·(number of inputs) bytes and hash_outputs hashes borsh of every output, so the cost of validating a transaction is (number of signature checks) × (size of the transaction), i.e. O(n²). The whole point of the BIP-143 preimage shape is to make this O(n) by hashing those three digests once per transaction, and crates/script/src/sighash.rs:34-35 explicitly claims that property: "hash_prevouts / hash_sequences / hash_outputs are precomputed digests, so signing n inputs is O(n) rather than Bitcoin's legacy O(n²)." They are not precomputed. The doc comment states a guarantee the code does not provide, which is how this survives review.
concrete_failure: A single transaction with 6,900 P2PKH inputs (≈145 wire bytes each, filling a 1,000,000-byte block) performs 6,900 CHECKSIGs, each re-hashing a 248 KB prevout concatenation → ≈1.7 GB of BLAKE3 that a cached implementation does in 248 KB. Amplify with multiple checks per input: 1,764 P2SH inputs (567 bytes each: 44 + a 523-byte push of a 520-byte redeem script) whose redeem script is `<65B sig> <32B pk>` followed by 66 repetitions of `OP_2DUP OP_CHECKSIG OP_DROP` stay inside MAX_OPS=201 and produce 1,764 × 66 ≈ 116,000 signature_hash calls over a 63 KB prevout digest ≈ 7.3 GB of hashing, on top of 116,000 Schnorr verifications — for one 1 MB block. The same script shape inside the 100,000-byte mempool standard-tx limit costs ≈11,600 signature checks per submission, and crates/mempool/src/pool/accept.rs has no rejection cache, so re-submitting the identical failing transaction repeats the full cost indefinitely.
suggested_fix: Compute hash_prevouts / hash_sequences / hash_outputs once per (transaction, sighash-type) and hand them to the VM: add an optional `SighashCache` to ExecCtx (or a `&mut` cache threaded through Machine) that memoises the three digests keyed by the ANYONECANPAY/NONE/SINGLE flavour, and have check_signature build only the fixed-width tail. Then either delete or correct the O(n) claim in the sighash module docs, and add a test asserting the digest count grows linearly, not quadratically, with input count.

title: max_peers is only checked on a peer's first connection, so one peer id can open unbounded connections
why_it_is_wrong: In `SwarmEvent::ConnectionEstablished` the worker increments `record.connections`, computes `let first = record.connections == 1`, and then `if !first { return; }` (events.rs:43-56) — returning *before* the `if self.peers.len() > self.max_peers` check on line 58. So the peer ceiling is only ever evaluated for the first connection of a given `PeerId`. `FerrumBehaviour` contains no `libp2p::connection_limits::Behaviour` (grep for `connection_limits`/`ConnectionLimits` in crates/p2p returns nothing) and `build_swarm` sets only `with_idle_connection_timeout`, so libp2p imposes no cap either. `self.peers.len()` counts distinct peer ids, so it never rises for a single-identity attacker.
concrete_failure: An attacker with one ed25519 keypair dials the node 10 000 times. Connection 1 is admitted (peers.len() == small). Connections 2..10 000 all take the `!first` early return and are never counted against `max_peers = 64` or closed. Each surviving connection holds a Noise session and a yamux session with `YAMUX_RECEIVE_WINDOW_BYTES = 4 MiB` of receive window plus up to `MAX_CONCURRENT_SYNC_STREAMS = 16` sync substreams; the attacker keeps each alive past `IDLE_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT` by opening a sync stream and stalling inside `read_frame`'s `read_exact` for the 30 s request timeout. Result: file-descriptor and memory exhaustion from a single identity, and the honest-peer ceiling is never enforced against it.
suggested_fix: Move the limit check above the `if !first` early return and enforce a per-peer established-connection cap (close any connection beyond, say, 2 per peer id), or add `libp2p::connection_limits::Behaviour` to `FerrumBehaviour` with both a global and a per-peer maximum.

title: bodies() materialises up to 64 full blocks (64 MB) before the 8 MiB byte budget trims the response
why_it_is_wrong: `bodies` applies only the COUNT cap: `for hash in hashes.iter().take(MAX_BLOCKS_SERVED)` with `MAX_BLOCKS_SERVED = 64` (serve.rs:89-97). The byte budget `MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES = 8 MiB` is applied later, in `SyncResponse::capped()` -> `cap_blocks` (p2p/src/message.rs:222-238), when the worker sends the response. With `max_block_size = 1 000 000 B` that means the node reads and decodes 64 blocks (~64 MB) and then throws ~56 of them away. The module doc at serve.rs:9-13 explicitly claims the opposite ("applies the same caps *before* building the response, so a peer asking for a million headers costs one bounded allocation rather than a large one that is then trimmed") — the claim holds for headers but not for bodies.
concrete_failure: A peer sends `GetBlocks` with 64 hashes of known full blocks. `serve::answer` reads and Borsh-decodes ~64 MB from redb, `cap_blocks` then truncates the vector to ~8 blocks, and 56 block reads plus their allocations are wasted. Repeated across the `MAX_CONCURRENT_SERVES = 8` permits this is ~512 MB of transient heap and 8x the necessary disk I/O per round, sustainable indefinitely by one peer at the cost of a 2 KB request — and it is what makes each serve slow enough for the event-loop stall in the `acquire_owned` finding to bite.
suggested_fix: Accumulate `block.serialized_size()` inside the `bodies` loop and stop as soon as the running total would exceed `MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES` (keeping at least one block, as `cap_blocks` does), so the byte budget is enforced before the read rather than after.

title: `finalized_height` fails open on a storage read error: the reorg-below-finality guard silently disappears and a committed prefix can be unwound
why_it_is_wrong: `finalized_from_view` derives finality entirely from `view.tip()` and `view.header_by_hash(&tip_hash)?`. The `HeaderView` contract turns every storage failure into `None`/a default — `StoreHeaderView::tip_or_default` (crates/chain/src/view.rs:52-61) logs a warning and returns `(BlockHash::ZERO, 0)` on a redb error, and `header_by_hash` returns `None` on error. crates/chain/src/view.rs's own module doc says "Failing closed is the only safe direction here", and for the difficulty rule it is — but for finality the polarity is inverted: a lower/absent value means *less* protection. Worse, the degradation compounds through the router: `EngineRouter::finalized_height` (crates/consensus/src/engine.rs:315-317) and the reorg guard in crates/chain/src/manager.rs:477-488 both do `let (_, tip_height) = view.tip();` and then `engine_for_height(tip_height)`, so a degraded tip of 0 selects the *PoW* engine, whose `finalized_height` is unconditionally `None`. There is no `unwrap_or(u64::MAX)`-style safe default anywhere on this path.
concrete_failure: Node with `bft_activation_height = Some(100)`, active tip at height 150, all of 100..150 sealed with verified 2f+1 certificates. A competing branch forking at height 120 with 31 blocks arrives, so `is_better` selects it and `reorganise` runs. `plan_reorg` succeeds (it reads the header table), then the guard opens a fresh `StoreHeaderView` and calls `view.tip()`, which reads `meta.tip` in a new redb read transaction. That read returns `Err` (transient I/O, file-lock contention, a temporarily exhausted handle) — `tip_or_default` logs "tip lookup failed; reporting an empty chain" and hands back `(ZERO, 0)`. `engine_for_height(0)` is the PoW engine, `finalized_height` is `None`, the `if let Some(finalized)` guard is skipped entirely, and `execute_reorg` proceeds to disconnect 30 BFT-committed blocks. The node's UTXO set now permanently disagrees with the rest of the validator set, and the only trace is one `warn` line.
suggested_fix: Do not let finality be inferred from a value that degrades to zero on error. Either widen the seam so the reorg guard can distinguish "tip unknown" from "tip at height 0" (e.g. a `try_tip() -> Result<...>` on `HeaderView`, or have `finalized_from_view` return `Some(u64::MAX)` when the tip hash is known-nonzero but its header cannot be read), or — simpler and local to the chain layer — make crates/chain/src/manager.rs read the tip from the authoritative `self.tip` cache / `self.store.tip()?` and propagate the storage error instead of running the reorg with a defaulted view.

title: A failure inside the disconnect loop leaves the chain half-rewound with no rollback and a stale tip cache
why_it_is_wrong:
`execute_reorg`'s disconnect loop propagates with `?`:
```rust
for expected in &plan.disconnect {
    let got = store.disconnect_tip()?;   // <- no roll_back on this path
```
The very next branch (`got != *expected`) does call `roll_back(store, params, engines, &[], &undone)`, so the intent is clearly to restore — the `?` skips it. Each `disconnect_tip` is its own committed transaction, so N-1 blocks may already be off the active chain when the Nth fails (`StorageError::Db`, `MissingUndo`, `MissingBlock`). Compounding it, `ChainManager::reorganise` propagates that error at manager.rs:491 *before* `self.refresh_tip()` at line 492, so the `RwLock<TipState>` cache still names the pre-reorg tip while `meta.tip` names something several blocks lower.
concrete_failure: Reorg plan disconnects [A6, A5, A4]. `disconnect_tip()` succeeds for A6 and A5, then fails for A4 with a redb IO error. `execute_reorg` returns Err with the store tip at A4 (height 4) and A6/A5 still off the chain, unrestored. `reorganise` returns without refreshing, so `ChainManager::tip()` still reports A6/height 6. The next honest block A7 arrives: `accept_locked` sees `prev_hash == incumbent.hash` (A6), calls `connect_tip_block`, and `Store::connect_block` rejects it with `NonContiguousConnect { tip_height: 4, height: 7 }`. That error then flows into `mark_invalid(&A7)` (finding 3), permanently poisoning a perfectly valid block — and the same happens to every subsequent block until the process is restarted.
suggested_fix: Wrap the disconnect loop so any error runs `roll_back(store, params, engines, &[], &undone)` before returning, mirroring the `got != *expected` branch. Independently, call `self.refresh_tip()` on the error path of `reorganise` (and after a failed `connect_tip_block` in `accept_locked`) so the cache can never claim a tip the store does not have.

title: Index maintenance is gated on a runtime flag that is never persisted or checked, so tx_index/addr_index silently diverge from the chain
why_it_is_wrong: `connect_block` (store.rs:335) and `disconnect_tip` (store.rs:410) both maintain `tx_index`/`addr_index` only `if self.cfg.index_transactions`. That flag comes from the command line (`crates/node/src/config.rs:256`) and is written nowhere in `meta` — the only meta keys are `tip`, `chain_id`, `schema_version` and `engine` (`crates/storage/src/tables.rs:87-94`). `Store::init` reconciles schema version and chain id but not this. Meanwhile `require_index()` (store.rs:456) gates the *readers* on the same runtime flag, so a store whose index is stale answers reads as if it were authoritative: `tx_location` returns `Ok(None)` ("not found") or a `TxLocation` naming a block that is no longer on the active chain, with no way for the caller to tell.
concrete_failure: Run `chaind --index` and sync to height 100; `tx_index` is complete. Restart without `--index` and let a 3-block reorg happen at the tip: `disconnect_tip` skips `index::unindex_block`, so `tx_index` keeps rows for the three orphaned blocks, and `connect_block` skips `index_block`, so the three replacement blocks are never indexed. Restart with `--index` again. `getrawtransaction`/`gettxlocation` for a transaction T that only ever existed in an orphaned block now returns `TxLocation { block_hash: <block not on any chain>, index }` — the explorer shows T as confirmed at a height where it does not exist — while transactions in the three new blocks report "not found". `address_history` lists the reorged-away txids in the same way. Nothing warns the operator, and `chain reindex` is the only fix.
suggested_fix: Record the index state in `meta` (e.g. `meta.index_transactions` plus the height it is complete to) on first write, and have `Store::init` refuse to open with `index_transactions: true` against a database whose recorded state disagrees — a typed `StorageError` telling the operator to run `chain reindex`, exactly as `SchemaMismatch` and `ChainIdMismatch` already do. Symmetrically, opening without `--index` against an indexed store should either keep maintaining the tables or clear the recorded flag.

title: Faucet quota is spent when the mempool rejects the payment, and two requests per block interval always conflict
why_it_is_wrong: The limiter is documented as "a quota is spent only on a payment that was actually made", and `Faucet::dispense` rolls back both keys when `build_payment` fails (crates/rpc/src/faucet.rs:283-289). But the REST handler calls `mempool.submit(...)` *after* `dispense` has returned, and a failure there propagates out with no rollback. And a failure there is not rare: `NodeKeyFaucetSource::spendable` selects from `chain.utxos_for_scripts`, which reads only the confirmed UTXO store (adapters.rs:147, `store.iter_utxos()`), never the mempool, and the source holds no reservation state of any kind. So a second request before the previous faucet tx is mined re-selects the same outpoint and builds a conflicting transaction, which `insert_one` refuses with `MempoolError::Conflict` (accept.rs:101 — no RBF in v1).
concrete_failure: Devnet block interval N seconds, faucet defaults (address window 24h, IP allowance 5/hour). Alice POSTs `/api/faucet` at t=0 and is paid. Bob POSTs from a different IP for a different address at t=1s: `dispense` records both of Bob's hits, `build_payment` selects the same (still-confirmed-unspent) coinbase output Alice's tx spends, `mempool.submit` returns `Conflict`, and Bob gets an error. Bob's address has now burned its 24-hour quota and his IP one of five hourly slots, with zero coins delivered. On a chain whose blocks are minutes apart, every request after the first in each interval fails this way.
suggested_fix: Move the mempool submission inside the rolled-back region (or have the handler call a `Faucet::rollback(&address_key, &ip_key, now)` on a submit failure), and give `NodeKeyFaucetSource` a set of outpoints it has already spent into an unconfirmed transaction, cleared when they leave the UTXO set — the same job `CoinCache::reserve` does for `Wallet`.

title: node.key and validator key files are created world-readable and chmod'd only afterwards
why_it_is_wrong: `NodeKey::write` does `std::fs::write(path, text)` and *then* `set_owner_only(path)` (0600). `write_key_file` in crates/cli/src/keyfile.rs:117-118 has the identical shape for the mnemonic key file. `std::fs::write` creates with `0o666 & ~umask` — 0644 under the usual umask — so between the create and the `chmod` the file is world-readable, and a descriptor opened inside that window keeps read access after the mode change (permissions are checked at open, not at read). The doc comments claim the file "is created with mode 0600", which is not what the code does. On the `keyfile.rs` path a `set_permissions` failure is only logged, so the 0644 file is left in place and the command still reports success.
concrete_failure: On a multi-user Linux host, an attacker runs a loop that `open(2)`s `<datadir>/node.key` as soon as it appears (inotify or a tight poll) while the operator does the very first `chaind --datadir /srv/ferrum --mine`. The open succeeds during the write→chmod window; the attacker reads the 32-byte hex seed, from which `m/44'/7767'/0'/0/0` is the address every coinbase pays and the address the faucet spends from, and `m/44'/7767'/1'/0/0` is the node's libp2p identity. The operator sees nothing: the file ends up 0600 and the node logs "generated a new node key".
suggested_fix: Create the file atomically with the final mode: on Unix use `std::fs::OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true).mode(0o600).open(path)` and write into that handle; keep `set_permissions` only as a repair for a pre-existing file. Apply the same to `keyfile::write_key_file`, and make a failure to restrict permissions on a freshly created secret an error rather than a warning.

title: The reference publishes the coinbase's outputs into the block overlay and production does not — an accept/reject split once coinbase_maturity is 0, and a wrong-variant split at every other maturity
why_it_is_wrong:
SPEC §3.3 rule 12 says non-coinbase transactions are applied "in block order, so a transaction may spend an output created by an earlier transaction in the same block". The coinbase is transaction 0. reference.rs:368-381 implements that literally: every coinbase output is `state.create(...)` before the transaction loop begins. crates/chain/src/apply.rs:299-304 deliberately does the opposite — "Returns the coins the coinbase creates... They are *not* added to the overlay" — so a spend of the block's own coinbase reads as absent rather than as immature.

The two executors therefore give different verdicts for the same block, and at the shipped devnet/mainnet maturities they at least agree it is invalid. They do not agree once maturity is 0: reference resolves the coin, computes `matures_at = height + 0 = height`, finds `height < height` false, and lets the spend through to the script and value rules — while production still says MissingInput. crates/chain/src/tests/reorg_tests.rs already runs the suite with `coinbase_maturity = 1`, so a 0 is one `devnet_with` closure away.

Nothing in the harness can reach this: chain_builder only ever hands out coins via `mature()`/`take_mature()`, which read `self.spendable` (populated on connect), and no fixture in mutate.rs or scenarios/ constructs a transaction spending a coinbase from its own block.
concrete_failure: At any height h in testing/sim with an honest coinbase C: build a non-coinbase transaction whose single input is `OutPoint::new(txid(C), 0)` and put it at index 1 of the block. `apply_block` returns `Err(MissingInput { tx_index: 1, out_point })`; `apply_block_reference` returns `Err(ImmatureCoinbaseSpend { coin_height: h, spend_height: h, maturity: 10 })`. With `params.coinbase_maturity = 0` the reference accepts the block outright and production still rejects it — a straight accept/reject disagreement between the two implementations of the seam.
suggested_fix: Pick one reading and make both match: either add the coinbase's coins to `OverlayView` in apply_block (SPEC's literal wording, maturity then does the rejecting) or amend SPEC §3.3 rule 12 to say the coinbase's outputs are not visible inside its own block and drop the `state.create` at reference.rs:370-381. Then add the fixture — a block whose tx1 spends its own coinbase — to invalid_variants so the choice is enforced.

title: Rule 15 (created outpoint must not already exist) runs inside the per-transaction loop in production and last in the reference; the only fixture that reaches it is the one case where the two orders coincide
why_it_is_wrong:
SPEC §3.3 and CONTRACT §8.1 both put "no created output already exists" last — after the coinbase's value and BIP-34 rules. reference.rs:511-519 does that: one pass over `created` against the pre-state after CoinbaseOverpayment has been decided. Production checks it per output, inside the rule-12 loop (apply.rs:189-192), i.e. strictly before rules 13 and 14, and again for the coinbase inside check_coinbase (apply.rs:328-332).

testing/sim/src/scenarios/duplicate_txid.rs::colliding_outpoint is the only fixture that reaches rule 15, and it seeds the collision on the *coinbase's* outpoint — the one position where production's check (inside check_coinbase, after the value rule) and the reference's (at the end) happen to fire in the same relative order. A collision on a non-coinbase output, which is the case the SPEC says rule 15 is kept for ("it also covers the case of a non-coinbase transaction colliding with an existing outpoint"), is never built.
concrete_failure: Seed the pre-state with a coin at `OutPoint::new(txid(tx1), 0)` for a non-coinbase tx1 the block will contain (the same trick colliding_outpoint already uses, applied to tx1 instead of the coinbase), and build the block with `coinbase_bonus: 1`. `apply_block` returns `Err(DuplicateOutPoint { out_point })` from apply.rs:191; `apply_block_reference` returns `Err(CoinbaseOverpayment { .. })` from reference.rs:506, because its rule-15 pass has not run yet. `judge()` reports ExecutorDisagreement.
suggested_fix: Move the non-coinbase rule-15 check out of the loop in apply_block into a final pass over the diff's `created`, matching SPEC's ordering and the reference; or record the deviation in SPEC §3.3 and reorder reference.rs to match. Add a non-coinbase collision fixture to scenarios/duplicate_txid.rs so the rule the SPEC says is kept for that case is actually exercised.

title: apply_block is never differentially tested under the BFT engine: sim_params leaves bft_activation_height unset, so ctx.engine_id is ENGINE_POW for every block the harness ever produces
why_it_is_wrong:
`sim_params()` (chain_builder.rs:60-67) starts from `ChainParams::devnet()`, which has `bft_activation_height: None` (crates/types/src/params.rs:213), and `ChainBuilder::ctx_for` builds every context with `BlockCtx::new(...)`, which derives `engine_id` from `params.engine_at(height)` (crates/chain/src/ctx.rs:56). So every ctx in the sim is PoW. Grepping the chain crate confirms no test anywhere constructs a `BlockCtx` with `engine_id == ENGINE_BFT` and calls `apply_block` — the only ENGINE_BFT use in crates/chain/src/tests is apply_tests.rs:291, which puts a BFT *seal* on a block in a PoW *context* to trigger WrongEngine.

That leaves the BFT arm of the seam with zero coverage, and it is not an empty arm: apply.rs:250 gates the whole target block (`compact_to_target`, ZeroTarget, TargetAbovePowLimit, hash_meets_target) on `engine_id == ENGINE_POW`, while reference.rs:209-224 runs compact_to_target / ZeroTarget / TargetAbovePowLimit unconditionally for every engine. SPEC §9.3 asks for a test that "asserts height h-1 validates under PoW and height h under BFT"; crates/consensus/src/bft/tests/fork.rs covers that at the *engine* level only, never through apply_block.
concrete_failure: Take any honest block, set `params.bft_activation_height = Some(h)` so `ctx.engine_id == ENGINE_BFT`, give it an empty BFT seal, and set `header.bits` to a compact value above `pow_limit` (or a non-canonical/zero-mantissa encoding). `apply_block` returns `Ok(diff)` — it never looks at `bits` under BFT. `apply_block_reference` returns `Err(Header(TargetAbovePowLimit { .. }))`. The two implementations of the determinism seam disagree on accept-vs-reject, and no test in the workspace can observe it because no test ever builds a BFT BlockCtx.
suggested_fix: Give ChainBuilder a BFT mode (params with `bft_activation_height`, `bft_validators`, and a seal factory) and run at least one differential sweep and one honest/attack scenario across the activation boundary, so both executors are compared on the arm SPEC §9.3 promises is tested. Independently, decide whether apply_block should validate `bits` under BFT and make the two agree.

title: The crash-consistency suite crashes a hand-copied duplicate of connect_block, not connect_block, and the copy omits the transaction-index writes
why_it_is_wrong:
crates/storage/src/tests/crash.rs states the property as "The tip never points at a height whose diff was not fully applied" and calls it the reason `Store::connect_block` is designed as it is. But the crash injection never runs `connect_block`: `connect_block_then_crash` (store.rs:466-501) re-implements the writes by hand and then drops the transaction. What the test proves is that redb rolls back *that copy's* single write transaction.

The copy has already drifted. `connect_block` writes the transaction index when `cfg.index_transactions` is on (store.rs:335-338) and writes `META_ENGINE` alongside `META_TIP` (store.rs:342-344); the crash twin does neither. And the suite opens with `StoreConfig::default()`, which has `index_transactions` off (the indexed variant is a separate constructor at store.rs:77) — so the indexed connect path, the one a node run with `--index` uses, has no crash coverage at all, from either side.
concrete_failure: The assertion block at crash.rs:120-129 ("The uncommitted block left nothing at all behind") checks BLOCKS, UNDO, HEIGHT and UTXO. It cannot check the index tables, because the twin never writes them and the config never enables them. If `connect_block` were changed to commit the block/undo/height tables in one transaction and the UTXO+tip in a second — a plausible batching change — a crash between the commits would leave a store whose tip lags its UTXO set, and `fifty_interrupted_restarts_all_come_back_consistent` would still pass all fifty rounds, because the crash it injects still comes from the untouched single-transaction copy.
suggested_fix: Drive the crash from the real code path rather than a twin: give `connect_block` a `#[cfg(test)]` abort hook (an injection point that returns before `txn.commit()`), so the test exercises the production write sequence including `index::index_block` and `META_ENGINE`. Run at least the every-third round with `StoreConfig` indexing enabled and assert the index tables are also empty after the aborted block.

title: SPEC §3.3 rule 15 is checked against the post-spend overlay, so spending the colliding coin in the same block bypasses the BIP-30 backstop, and connect_block then silently overwrites
why_it_is_wrong: SPEC §3.3 rule 15 says "No created output already exists **in the UTXO set**", and §3.3 explains it is deliberately kept as redundant "defence in depth on the inflation path". Production checks it against the mutated OverlayView (apply.rs:190 for non-coinbase outputs, apply.rs:329 for coinbase outputs). OverlayView::has_coin returns false for any outpoint the same block already marked spent (crates/storage/src/view.rs, `Some(None) => Ok(false)`), so the rule is satisfied by simply spending the colliding coin earlier in the block. The reference executor written from SPEC checks `pre.has_coin(op)` against the parent state (testing/sim/src/reference.rs, "Rule 15 ... Checked against the *pre*-state"), so the two implementations disagree by construction. Compounding it, Store::connect_block (store.rs:326-331) applies `utxo.insert` for every created outpoint and then `utxo.remove` for every spent one, ignoring insert's returned old value — so a rule-15 miss is not merely accepted, it silently destroys a live coin and leaves the committed UTXO set disagreeing with the StateDiff apply_block returned.
concrete_failure: Block B at height h contains tx1 spending outpoint P (P is unspent in the parent UTXO set, value 10 FRM) and, later in the same block, a transaction whose txid equals P.txid so it re-creates P. apply_block: tx1's spend puts P in the overlay cache as `None`; when the later transaction's outputs are published, `overlay.has_coin(&P)` returns false, so no DuplicateOutPoint is raised and the block is ACCEPTED. apply_block_reference on the same inputs returns Err(DuplicateOutPoint { out_point: P }) — an accept-vs-reject split between the two executors. Store::connect_block then inserts the new coin at P (diff.created) and immediately removes P (diff.spent), so the block's own output vanishes: the node's UTXO set has neither the old coin nor the new one, while the StateDiff it just committed claims P was created. The identical shape applies to the coinbase via check_coinbase (apply.rs:329), where the destroyed coin is the whole subsidy+fees payout. Reachability today rests entirely on txid uniqueness (BIP-34 for coinbases, input-already-spent for non-coinbases) — i.e. exactly the single layer rule 15 exists to back up. The existing tests (spend_tests.rs `creating_an_outpoint_that_already_exists_is_rejected` and `a_non_coinbase_output_colliding_with_the_utxo_set_is_rejected`) both use a collision outpoint that is NOT spent in the block, so neither covers this path.
suggested_fix: Check rule 15 against the pre-state, not the overlay: keep a `&dyn StateView` handle on `pre` in apply_block and test `pre.has_coin(&out_point)` (matching reference.rs), or accumulate the block's created set separately and test `pre.has_coin(op) || created_set.contains(op)`. Separately, make Store::connect_block reject rather than clobber: inspect the value returned by `utxo.insert` and return a typed StorageError if a created outpoint already had a row.

title: submitblock bypasses check_future_time, the only block-entry path that does
why_it_is_wrong: SPEC §3.2 rule 10 (`timestamp_ms <= now + max_future_block_time_ms`) is a block-validation rule; it lives above the pure seam in Relay::accept_block_at (relay.rs:366) precisely because it needs a clock. Every other way a block enters the node goes through Relay: the miner (miner.rs:203 — its doc comment says "The block goes through the same Relay path as a block from the network — one implementation of 'what it means to accept a block', including the future-time check"), gossip (node/tasks.rs:243) and sync (sync.rs:429/472/505). The RPC adapter's submit_block calls `self.chain.accept_block(block)` directly, so rule 10 is simply never applied to an RPC-submitted block. That is a consensus rule enforced in one path and not another inside the same binary.
concrete_failure: An external miner (or `chain-cli`, or a misconfigured pool with a clock 3 hours fast) submits a block whose header.timestamp_ms is now+3h via `submitblock`. mainnet max_future_block_time_ms is 7_200_000 (2h). The receiving node accepts it — ChainManager::accept_block never consults a clock — makes it the tip, and gossips it. Every peer runs it through Relay::accept_block, gets ConsensusError::TimestampTooFarInFuture, returns GossipVerdict::Reject and scores the announcing peer down on gossipsub's P4. The submitting node then mines on a tip no peer will follow for the next hour, and its own subsequent blocks are orphaned by the network; the local node also had no chance to refuse its own bad block, which is exactly the failure the miner path documents itself as preventing.
suggested_fix: Route RPC submissions through the same seam as everything else: give the RPC adapter a Relay handle (or a clock) and call Relay::accept_block, so rule 10 is applied once, in one place, for every block entry point.
