If the adapter must stay chain-only, call ferrum_consensus::check_future_time(&block.header, clock.now_ms(), chain.params()) before accept_block and return the same non-recording rejection Relay does.

title: Production hides the coinbase's outputs from the block overlay while the reference executor publishes them, so the two executors reject a block that spends its own coinbase for different reasons
why_it_is_wrong: SPEC §3.3 rule 12 says non-coinbase transactions are validated "against an overlay of the UTXO set at the parent, applied in block order, so a transaction may spend an output created by an earlier transaction in the same block" — and the coinbase is transaction 0, i.e. earlier than everything. testing/sim/src/reference.rs:373-386 implements that literally: it does state.create() for every coinbase output before the tx loop, so a later tx resolves the coin and then fails the §4.2.2 maturity check. crates/chain/src/apply.rs deliberately does the opposite — check_coinbase's doc says the coins are "*not* added to the overlay" — so overlay.get_coin() misses and the same block is rejected as MissingInput. SPEC §3.4 makes the variant observable behaviour ("Tests assert the exact variant, not merely that validation failed"), and tests/differential.rs asserts exactly that with `"the two executors reject for different reasons"`. The divergence is not currently generated: mutate.rs:341-354 only builds the immature-spend case from a *previous* block's coinbase (`chain.spendable()`), never the block's own. The audit substitute therefore has a live, unexercised disagreement in it, and the two implementations do not agree on which SPEC rule this block breaks.
concrete_failure: Build any block at height H whose tx[1] spends OutPoint::new(txid(block.txs[0]), 0) — the coinbase of the very same block. ferrum_chain::apply_block returns ValidationError::MissingInput { tx_index: 1, out_point }; ferrum_sim::apply_block_reference returns ValidationError::ImmatureCoinbaseSpend { tx_index: 1, coin_height: H, spend_height: H, maturity: 10 }. Feed that block to differential.rs::agree() and it panics with "the two executors reject for different reasons at height H". The verdicts only coincide because coinbase_maturity >= 1 on all three networks; at maturity 0 production would still say MissingInput while the reference accepts the spend outright.
suggested_fix: Pick one reading and make both match. The SPEC text supports the reference: publish the coinbase's outputs into the OverlayView before the tx loop in apply_block (they are already computed for `created`), leaving §4.2.2 maturity as the rule that rejects the spend. Then add a mutation to testing/sim/src/mutate.rs that spends the block's own coinbase, so the differential harness actually covers it.

title: ExecStats is computed and thrown away: there is no per-transaction or per-block signature-check budget
why_it_is_wrong: verify() returns ExecStats { ops, max_stack, sig_checks } and its doc comment (crates/script/src/interpreter.rs:84-88) says it is "returned rather than logged so the mempool and the block validator can bill for it without re-running anything." Neither caller bills: crates/chain/src/apply.rs:171 and crates/mempool/src/pool/accept.rs:173 both discard the Ok value. MAX_OPS=201 is a *per-input* budget, and OP_CHECKMULTISIG charges only 1 + n for up to n verifications (crates/script/src/interpreter/ops.rs:369), so one input can demand ~190 Schnorr verifications. Crucially the expensive script can live entirely in the script_pubkey, which is already in the UTXO set, so the spending input costs as little as 44 bytes of block/transaction space — there is no proportionality between the bytes an attacker pays for and the verification work every node must do. Bitcoin closes exactly this gap with MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS; Ferrum has no equivalent constant anywhere (grep for 'sigop' across crates/ returns nothing).
concrete_failure: Given N previously-created UTXOs whose script_pubkeys each do ~190 signature checks within the 1,000-byte / 201-op limits (e.g. 20 pushed pubkeys + `<k>` + OP_CHECKMULTISIG repeated), a transaction spending them with empty script_sigs is 44·N bytes. At the mempool's MAX_STANDARD_TX_SIZE of 100,000 bytes that is ~2,270 inputs and ~430,000 Schnorr verifications for one 100 KB message — and because accept() reaches script verification at step 10 and keeps no rejection cache, an attacker re-sends the same transaction (which fails, so the UTXOs are never consumed) to burn that CPU on every node, repeatedly, for free. At block scale a 1,000,000-byte block of the same inputs demands ~1.5 million verifications, far beyond what the 120 s target spacing allows.
suggested_fix: Sum the returned ExecStats.sig_checks (and ops) across a transaction's inputs and across a block, and reject above a consensus constant — e.g. MAX_BLOCK_SIGCHECKS proportional to max_block_size, plus a per-transaction cap for relay policy. Add the constant to CONTRACT §5.1 so it is present rather than retrofitted, and add a test that a block exceeding the budget is rejected with a named error.

title: The script fuzz target does not compile, so the panic-freedom guarantee CONTRACT §5.4 rests on is never exercised
why_it_is_wrong: Line 21 is `use ferrum_script::{ExecCtx, Script, ScriptLimits};`, but `ferrum_script` exports no `Script`. crates/script/src/lib.rs:84-94 lists the complete public surface — ScriptError, ExecCtx/ExecStats/Stack/eval/is_p2sh/verify, the limits constants and ScriptLimits, ScriptNum/cast_to_bool/is_minimal_bool/is_minimally_encoded, Instruction/Opcode, disassemble/is_push_only/parse, SigHashType/sighash_preimage/signature_hash, ScriptType — and there is no `pub use ferrum_types::Script` and no `Script` type defined in the crate. The sibling target testing/fuzz/fuzz_targets/decode.rs correctly imports its types from ferrum_types. Nothing catches this because Cargo.toml:19 has `exclude = ["testing/fuzz"]`, so `cargo build`, `cargo test` and `cargo clippy` over the workspace never touch the file. CONTRACT §5.4 ("The interpreter must never panic on any input. A cargo-fuzz target asserts this") and SPEC §5 rule 9 both point at this target as the enforcement mechanism.
concrete_failure: `cargo +nightly fuzz build --fuzz-dir testing/fuzz script` fails with E0432 `unresolved import ferrum_script::Script`, so the target has never run. The `decode` target still builds, which makes the breakage easy to miss — a maintainer running the documented fuzz command for `decode` sees success and assumes both are healthy. The proptest suite in crates/script/tests/never_panics.rs (10,000 + 2,000 cases) is the only thing actually covering panic-freedom, and it is a bounded random sweep, not coverage-guided fuzzing.
suggested_fix: Change the import to `use ferrum_script::{ExecCtx, ScriptLimits};` and `use ferrum_types::{Amount, ChainId, OutPoint, Script, Transaction, TxIn, TxOut};`, then verify with `cargo +nightly fuzz build --fuzz-dir testing/fuzz`. Add a CI step (or a line in the Makefile's check target) that runs `cargo +nightly fuzz build --fuzz-dir testing/fuzz` so an excluded-from-workspace crate cannot silently rot again.

title: `record_commit` raises finality from an unverified certificate and can never be lowered, so one bad commit permanently bricks the node's fork choice
why_it_is_wrong: `record_commit` is `pub` and takes a `BftCommit` straight from the caller, writing `state.finalized = max(current, commit.height)` and `state.last_commit = Some(commit)` with no call to `verify_commit` — which is right there on the same type, is cheap, and is exactly what `seal()` runs before touching the same two fields (engine.rs:447-451). The doc comment ("Record a *verified* commit") pushes the obligation onto a driver that does not exist yet in this tree, so the invariant is currently unenforced and untested — `finality_follows_the_last_recorded_commit` (tests/fork.rs:324) in fact demonstrates the engine accepting a commit for height 41 over an arbitrary hash the view has never heard of. Because the update is a monotone `max`, the damage is irreversible for the lifetime of the process: there is no API that lowers `finalized`.
concrete_failure: A future driver (or an RPC/test harness) hands `record_commit` a certificate decoded from a peer's block seal before `validate_seal` has run on it — the natural ordering mistake, since the type is public and self-describing. The certificate claims `height: u64::MAX` with garbage signatures. `state.finalized` becomes `Some(u64::MAX)`, so `finalized_height` returns `u64::MAX` for the rest of the process, `EngineRouter::check_reorg` rejects every reorg at every depth with `ReorgBelowFinalized`, the node can never switch to the honest chain again, and `getblockchaininfo` reports `finalized_height: 18446744073709551615`. A restart is the only recovery, and it re-happens on the next such message.
suggested_fix: Make `record_commit` fallible and self-checking: `pub fn record_commit(&self, commit: BftCommit) -> Result<(), ConsensusError>` that calls `self.verify_commit(&commit, &commit.block_hash, commit.height)` before mutating `finalized`/`last_commit`. That is the same guard `seal()` already applies to its own certificate, costs `2f+1` Schnorr verifications, and makes the "verified" in the doc comment enforced rather than aspirational.

title: Mnemonic::from_entropy builds the phrase in a growing plain String, leaving unzeroized prefixes in freed heap
why_it_is_wrong: The module contract is "the phrase is held in a `Zeroizing<String>`", and `Mnemonic` is declared zeroizing in CONTRACT §4. But `from_entropy` starts with `String::new()` (zero capacity) and grows it with `push_str` for each word, wrapping in `Zeroizing` only at the end. `String` reallocates geometrically, and each reallocation copies the bytes into a new buffer and frees the old one **without zeroizing it** — `Zeroizing<String>` can only scrub the buffer that is live at drop. `from_phrase` is fine (`words.join(" ")` allocates once at the exact size), so this is specific to the generation path, which is exactly the path `Wallet::create` → `Mnemonic::generate` takes for every new wallet.
concrete_failure: `chain-cli wallet new` generates a 12-word phrase of ~85 bytes. The String's capacity walks 0→8→16→32→64→128; the 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-byte buffers are freed with plaintext in them and only the 128-byte one is scrubbed. A core dump, a swapped page, or a heap-reuse read of that process therefore yields a 64-byte prefix — the first nine words of the twelve. The remaining three words are 33 bits minus the 4 checksum bits ≈ 2^29 candidates, an offline search well within reach, so the whole wallet is recoverable from a fragment the code believes it erased.
suggested_fix: Build into a zeroizing buffer sized up front: `let mut phrase = Zeroizing::new(String::with_capacity(word_count * 9));` (the longest BIP-39 English word is 8 chars plus a separator), so no reallocation ever happens and the single buffer is the one that gets scrubbed.

title: The validator key and node key are read into non-zeroizing Strings
why_it_is_wrong: `load_validator_key` does `std::fs::read_to_string(path)` and passes the plain `String` to `parse_validator_key`, which may hold a full BIP-39 mnemonic or a raw 32-byte hex scalar. Nothing zeroizes it; it is dropped as an ordinary heap allocation. `NodeKey::load_or_create` (crates/node/src/node/keys.rs:99) has the same shape for the seed hex. The CLI's equivalent reader takes care to wrap the text in `Zeroizing` (crates/cli/src/keyfile.rs:66-69), so this is an inconsistency in handling the identical material rather than an accepted trade-off. `parse_validator_key` is also `pub`, so a caller can pass it a `&str` it cannot scrub either.
concrete_failure: `chaind --validator-key /srv/ferrum/validator.key` where the file holds the mnemonic `wallet new --output` wrote. Every node start leaves the full twelve- or twenty-four-word BFT signing mnemonic in freed heap for the life of the process; a core dump taken later (a panic with `ulimit -c unlimited`, or a crash reporter) contains it in plaintext, even though the derived `SecretKey` itself zeroizes on drop and the seed is explicitly scrubbed two lines later.
suggested_fix: Read the bytes and wrap immediately — `let text = Zeroizing::new(String::from_utf8(std::fs::read(path)?)...)` — and take `&str` in `parse_validator_key` only from that guarded value, matching what `crates/cli/src/keyfile.rs::load_key_file` already does.

title: The `check` field is outside the MAC, so a corrupted keystore is reported as a wrong passphrase
why_it_is_wrong: `mac_message` covers version, chain id, kdf algorithm, cipher name, iterations, salt, nonce, the three `meta` counters and the ciphertext — but **not** `check`. `Keystore::open` compares `check` first and returns `WrongPassphrase` on a mismatch, before the MAC is ever evaluated. The module's stated property #3 is "a separate check value distinguishes a typo from tampering… a user who mistyped should not be told their file is corrupt"; because `check` is unauthenticated, the implication runs the other way too and a damaged file is reported as a mistyped passphrase, which is the more dangerous of the two errors to get wrong.
concrete_failure: A single bit flips in the 64 hex characters of `"check"` (bad sector, a truncated sync, an editor that rewrote the JSON). `Keystore::open` derives the correct keys, finds `keys[64..] != stored_check`, and returns `WrongPassphrase`. `open_existing` (crates/cli/src/commands/wallet.rs:70-76) then re-prompts on the terminal, and every passphrase the user types is rejected the same way. The user concludes they have forgotten their passphrase — while the ciphertext and MAC are intact and the wallet is fully recoverable by ignoring `check`. A user who reacts by `wallet new --force` deletes the only copy of their key.
suggested_fix: Include `check` in `mac_message` (length-prefixed, alongside salt and nonce) and, when the check comparison fails, verify the MAC before choosing the error: MAC valid → `WrongPassphrase`; MAC invalid → `KeystoreCorrupt`. That makes the two errors actually mean what the module documentation says they mean.

title: The differential sweep never asserts which rule a named mutation breaks, and its coverage floor collapses all header and seal rules into two buckets
why_it_is_wrong:
`agree()` asserts only that the two executors return the same thing, and the sweep then asserts `verdict.is_err()`. Nowhere does it say that the mutation named "the timestamp is not strictly after median time past" is actually rejected as `TimestampTooOld` — any shared rejection satisfies both assertions. mutate.rs's own unit test (`every_variant_is_rejected_by_production`) is weaker still: `is_err()` only.

The backstop is `variants_seen.len() >= 15`, but `variant_name` (differential.rs:180-215) maps every `ValidationError::Header(_)` to the single string "Header" and every `Seal(_)` to "Seal". Six of the catalogue's mutations — bad version, wrong parent, timestamp too old, insufficient work, non-empty PoW seal, wrong engine — therefore contribute two buckets between them. This is exactly the shape SPEC §3.4 warns about ("A test that only asserts 'rejected' passes when the block is rejected for the wrong reason, which is how a rule silently stops being tested") in the file that exists to enforce §3.4.
concrete_failure: If `grind_until_invalid` (mutate.rs:104-115) ever stopped finding a failing nonce for the sim's near-max target and returned the ground header unchanged, the "the header hash does not meet its target" mutation would become an entirely valid block. Both executors would then agree it is *valid*, `verdict.is_err()` would fail — but the milder version of the same failure does pass silently: if that mutation instead started tripping BadVersion or WrongParent, both executors would still agree, the verdict would still be an error, and `variants_seen` would still contain "Header", so the PoW rule would stop being differentially tested with no test turning red.
suggested_fix: Add an expected-variant field to `Mutation` in testing/sim/src/mutate.rs and assert it in the sweep (`assert!(matches!(verdict, Err(expected)))`), the way the scenario modules already do. Expand `variant_name` to name the inner `ConsensusError` for Header/Seal so the coverage floor counts distinct header rules instead of one bucket.

title: Coinbase outputs never enter the validation overlay, so apply_block and the reference executor disagree about a same-block spend of the coinbase
why_it_is_wrong: SPEC §3.3 rule 12 says non-coinbase transactions are validated "against an overlay of the UTXO set at the parent, applied in block order, so a transaction may spend an output created by an earlier transaction in the same block" — and the coinbase is transaction 0, i.e. an earlier transaction. The reference executor implements exactly that: it `state.create(...)`s every coinbase output before the tx loop (testing/sim/src/reference.rs:369-381). Production does the opposite: check_coinbase runs *after* the loop (apply.rs:198) and its comment states the coinbase coins are "*not* added to the overlay". The rule that is supposed to stop a same-block coinbase spend is coinbase maturity (§4.2.2), not outpoint absence, and production replaces one rule with another.
concrete_failure: A block at height h whose coinbase creates P = (txid(coinbase), 0) and whose tx1 spends P. apply_block returns Err(MissingInput { tx_index: 1, out_point: P }); apply_block_reference resolves P, sees is_coinbase, and returns Err(ImmatureCoinbaseSpend { coin_height: h, spend_height: h, maturity }). differential.rs::agree does `assert_eq!(a, b, "the two executors reject for different reasons ...")` on the exact ValidationError variant, so this block would fail the differential test; it is latent only because ChainBuilder's workload spends only `chain.take_mature(...)` coins and mutate.rs never builds one. With `coinbase_maturity = 0` — a legal value of the public `ChainParams::coinbase_maturity` field, which chain tests already override — the divergence becomes accept-vs-reject: mature_at == h, so the reference ACCEPTS the block while production still rejects it with MissingInput.
suggested_fix: Publish the coinbase's outputs into the overlay before the non-coinbase loop (splitting check_coinbase into a structural/BIP-34 pass up front and the value check afterwards), so the maturity rule — not an accidental absence — is what rejects a same-block coinbase spend. Add a mutate.rs variant "a transaction spends this block's own coinbase" so the harness pins the chosen variant.

title: check_header applies the median-time-past rule before the target and proof-of-work rules, contradicting SPEC §3.2, CONTRACT §8.1 and the reference executor
why_it_is_wrong: SPEC §3.2 fixes the order as rule 7 (`bits`), rule 8 (proof of work), rule 9 (`timestamp_ms > MTP*1000`), and states plainly that "an implementation that checks them in a *different* order can accept a block another node rejects if two rules disagree"; §3.4 requires tests to assert the exact variant. CONTRACT §8.1 rule 5 lists "PoW target met; bits equals next_bits(parent); timestamp_ms > median_time_past(parent) * 1000" in that order. The reference executor follows the documents (testing/sim/src/reference.rs:208-240: target expansion, ZeroTarget, TargetAbovePowLimit, InsufficientWork, then TimestampTooOld). Production inverts it: apply.rs:242-248 raises TimestampTooOld before the `if ctx.engine_id == ENGINE_POW` target block at apply.rs:250-266. A second, separate inversion sits at apply.rs:218-228: the version check runs *before* the genesis exemption, while the reference takes the genesis early-return first (reference.rs:189-197) and therefore never checks the version for genesis at all.
concrete_failure: A block whose header carries `bits` above `params.pow_limit` and `timestamp_ms == ctx.median_time_past_ms()`: apply_block returns Err(Header(TimestampTooOld{..})) while apply_block_reference returns Err(Header(TargetAbovePowLimit{..})). differential.rs::agree asserts the two error values are equal, so this block fails the audit-substitute test. Second scenario: a genesis-context block (ctx.height == 0) with header.version = 0 — production returns Err(Header(BadVersion(0))), the reference returns Ok(()). Both are latent purely because mutate.rs is built so that "every entry breaks **exactly one** rule", so no fixture ever exercises two header rules at once.
suggested_fix: Reorder check_header to match SPEC §3.2 / CONTRACT §8.1: parentage, then target expansion + pow_limit + proof of work, then the median-time-past bound; and move the `version < MIN_BLOCK_VERSION` test to whichever side of the genesis exemption the documents intend (fix the reference if genesis really is exempt). Add a mutate.rs entry or a direct unit test that breaks two header rules at once so the chosen order is pinned.

title: The target and pow_limit checks are gated on engine_id == ENGINE_POW, so at a BFT height apply_block accepts a header with a zero or over-limit target that the reference rejects
why_it_is_wrong: apply.rs:250 wraps the whole target block — `compact_to_target(header.bits)`, the ZeroTarget check and the TargetAbovePowLimit check — inside `if ctx.engine_id == BlockSeal::ENGINE_POW`. The reference executor expands and range-checks the target for every engine and gates only `hash_meets_target` on PoW (reference.rs:208-231). Under BFT, production therefore performs no validation of `header.bits` at all inside the seam, even though `bits` is a hashed header field that every node must agree on. apply.rs's own module doc claims the function "re-checks every rule it *can* see ... so that it is a complete and self-contained verdict for the differential harness and for any caller that holds only a pre-state", which is not true here.
concrete_failure: With `params.bft_activation_height = Some(h)` and a block at height h whose header carries `bits = CompactTarget(0)` (or any compact value expanding above `params.pow_limit`), apply_block returns Ok(diff) while apply_block_reference returns Err(Header(ZeroTarget)) / Err(Header(TargetAbovePowLimit{..})) — a production-accepts/reference-rejects split, the case differential.rs panics on with "production accepted but the reference rejected". A node is still protected because ChainManager calls ConsensusEngine::validate_header (which requires `bits == next_bits(parent)`) before apply_block, and no shipped ChainParams sets bft_activation_height, so this is latent rather than exploitable today.
suggested_fix: Move the `compact_to_target` / ZeroTarget / TargetAbovePowLimit checks out of the `engine_id == ENGINE_POW` guard and keep only `hash_meets_target` inside it, matching reference.rs:208-231, so `bits` is validated at every height under every engine.

title: apply_block skips target expandability and the pow_limit bound for non-PoW engines and orders the version check differently around the genesis exemption; the reference executor does neither
why_it_is_wrong: check_header() puts the whole `compact_to_target` / ZeroTarget / TargetAbovePowLimit block inside `if ctx.engine_id == BlockSeal::ENGINE_POW`, and it checks `version < MIN_BLOCK_VERSION` before the `ctx.is_genesis()` early return. reference_check_header (testing/sim/src/reference.rs:198-235) does the reverse on both counts: it returns early for genesis before looking at version, and it expands and range-checks `bits` for every engine, gating only the hash comparison on ENGINE_POW. apply_block is documented as "a complete and self-contained verdict for the differential harness and for any caller that holds only a pre-state", so these are two implementations of the same seam that disagree on verdicts, not just on ordering. In production the disagreement is currently unreachable (BftEngine::next_bits returns the parent's bits, which is always a valid target inherited from the last PoW block, and genesis is always built with GENESIS_VERSION = 1), and testing/sim never generates a BFT-engine ctx (mutate.rs:262 is the only BFT mention and it is a WrongEngine case), so nothing exercises it today.
concrete_failure: Call ferrum_chain::apply_block with a BlockCtx whose engine_id is BlockSeal::ENGINE_BFT on a block whose header.bits is CompactTarget(0x00800000) (the negative form) or 0x2100ffff (above every pow_limit): production returns Ok(diff) — it never touches bits — while ferrum_sim::apply_block_reference returns Err(ValidationError::Header(ConsensusError::NegativeTarget)) / TargetAbovePowLimit. Symmetrically, a genesis block (height 0) with header.version = 0 gives production Err(Header(BadVersion(0))) and the reference Ok. Either case makes tests/differential.rs::agree panic with "production accepted but the reference rejected" / "the reference accepted but production rejected" the moment a BFT or malformed-genesis ctx is added to the harness.
suggested_fix: Move the `compact_to_target` / is_zero / pow_limit checks out of the ENGINE_POW branch in apply.rs::check_header so `bits` is always a well-formed, in-range target regardless of engine, and keep only `hash_meets_target` engine-gated; and put the genesis early-return in the same position in both files (SPEC §2 exempts genesis from PoW-vs-parent, the difficulty transition and MTP — not from the version rule, so production's order is the right one and the reference should follow it).

title: templates::cltv_p2pkh and templates::htlc emit scripts that classify() calls NonStandard once the locktime needs five bytes, so the mempool refuses to relay outputs the library itself builds
why_it_is_wrong: push_as_num() decodes the locktime operand with `ScriptNum::from_slice(data, 4, true)` — a four-byte ceiling. But cltv_p2pkh (:151) and htlc (:189) take a `u32` and encode it with `push_num` → `ScriptNum::to_vec()`, which for any value ≥ 0x8000_0000 produces five bytes (sign-magnitude needs the extra sign byte). The interpreter is consistent with the builder here — check_lock_time reads the operand at max_locktime_num_size() = 5 (crates/script/src/interpreter/ops.rs:418) — but the classifier is not, so a script the VM executes happily is labelled NonStandard. crates/mempool/src/policy.rs:162 (`is_standard_output`) rejects any output classify() names NonStandard, and mempool accept step 4 runs that check.
concrete_failure: `templates::classify(&templates::cltv_p2pkh(2_147_483_648, &pkh))` returns ScriptType::NonStandard instead of ScriptType::Cltv: push_as_num on the 5-byte operand returns Err(NumTooLarge{len:5,max:4}) → None → the `i.len() == 8` CLTV arm short-circuits and the function falls through to NonStandard. A transaction paying to that script is then rejected by the mempool with NonStandardOutput and never relayed, even though `verify` would execute it and the same script with locktime 2_147_483_647 relays fine. `templates::htlc(&h, &r, 2_147_483_648, &f)` fails identically via is_htlc's push_as_num(i.get(10)) at :318. (Timestamp locktimes cross 0x8000_0000 in January 2038.)
suggested_fix: Give the classifier a locktime-specific reader that uses MAX_LOCKTIME_NUM_SIZE (5) rather than the arithmetic ceiling of 4 — e.g. a `push_as_locktime_num` helper used by the Cltv arm at :290 and by is_htlc at :318 — so classify() accepts exactly the operand widths check_lock_time accepts. Add a round-trip test asserting `classify(cltv_p2pkh(t, &pkh)) == ScriptType::Cltv` for t across the 0x7fff_ffff boundary, and the same for htlc.
